newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai markets slump after finance chief quits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai markets slump after finance chief quits.

text.p: Thailand's embattled finance minister resigned on Thursday, sending the currency and stock markets into a nose dive, but Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh promised to name a quick replacement to oversee the troubled economy.

Seeking to calm nervous markets, Chavalit also said there would be no change in the current policy of defending the Thai baht and that finance and foreign exchange stability were the government's top priority.

The stock market tumbled to a fresh eight-year low following Amnuay Viravan's resignation on a hectic day of selling by nervous punters concerned about the future course of the government's economic policy, brokers said. The index ended 3.76 percent down at 464.77.
The baht recovered somewhat after an early dive and in the offshore market was quoted at 25.150/650 late on Thursday against 26.500/27.500 earlier in the day.
Chavalit said his new finance minister, who he expected to name on Friday, would not be a politician.
"The public tend not to trust politicians for this portfolio. Therefore, we will opt for a competent outsider," he told a news conference.
Government sources and analysts told Reuters that Chavalit's list of candidates for the tough finance job ranged from eminent bankers to former ministers.

Amnuay, a non-elected member of the cabinet, quit because of political differences with rivals in the six-party coalition government over his management of the economy which is in its worst slump in more than a decade.
He left after losing an intra-government battle over a plan to raise excise taxes for some consumer items.
Thailand has had five finance ministers in three governments since 1995.
Among prospective candidates for the post were deputy central bank governor Chaiwat Wibulsawasdi and Olarn Chaiprawat, top executive at Siam Commercial Bank, analysts said
Others were Virapongsa Ramangura, a former finance minister, the chief of state-run Exim Bank, Pridiyathorn Devakul, and ex-banker and communications minister, Vichit Surapongchai.
Brokers said stocks were expected to decline further on Friday but much depended on who would replace Amnuay.

"Investors are watching whether the new finance minister would be capable enough to handle economic problems or not. The market is likely to decline heavily if the new minister is unacceptable to the public," said Somnuk Chnrasamee, analyst at Nava Finance and Securities.
Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee, who was chosen by Amnuay to be part of his economic team, said he would also resign on June 21.

Chavalit said there would be no changes in the government's approach to managing the economy after Amnuay's departure. He would defend the baht against foreign speculative attacks as Amnuay had done previously.
Earlier, the baht slid because of worries a devaluation might follow after Amnuay left, dealers said.

"The important thing is that we will carry out measures that have been started, especially in the policy of fixing the baht where there will not be any change. And the new finance minister will continue this policy," Chavalit said.

Thailand's finance and property sectors have been hit by bad loans and a liquidity crunch, the baht has come under speculative attack, consumer and investment spending has slowed and exports have fallen.
Economic growth this year is seen officially at 5.9 percent, the slowest in more than a decade, against 6.4 percent in 1996. Economists see growth even lower at between three and five percent.
Amnuay gave a parting warning about the severe Thai economic downturn and his departure.
"I would like to remind that change in the economic field is a sensitive one because it is linked to the fate of the private sector, the government and the stability of the overall economy," he said.
